newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court condemns Philip Morris on ads.
newsitem.headline: French court condemns Philip Morris on ads.

text.p: A civil law court on Wednesday found U.S. tobacco-maker Philip Morris guilty of violating a French ban on touting smoking but fined the company just one franc (18 cents) in damages.

The conviction came in a legal challenge to a series of controversial newspaper advertisements filed by the National Committee against Tobacco Use and the European Union of Non-Smokers, which had sought three million francs ($542,000) in damages and interest.

The ads, which appeared in a number of French newspapers over several weeks, bemoaned the growing regulation of tobacco products around the world and questioned where it would all end. Some of the ads were published in other European cities as well.
One of the contested ads showed a map of Paris divided in two, with one half a smoking zone and the other for non-smokers.
"How far will they go?" asked the advertisement.
Another showed smokers forced out of their offices and asked: "What is this policy which is forcing people outside?"
A 1991 law prohibits all direct or indirect advertising for tobacco, and French Health Minister Herve Gaymard denounced the Philip Morris campaign in June.
The tobacco giant argued the ads were political commentary, but the court concluded they "encouraged smokers to consume tobacco".

Another Paris court had in June banned other ads in the Philip Morris campaign which compared the risk of lung cancer from breathing in second-hand smoke to the danger of heart disease from eating biscuits or drinking milk.
The court in that case was acting on a complaint by French biscuit makers that the ads were harmful to biscuit sales.
